chunks: "Sharper edges are good for timing and bad for noise, so it's a trade-off I try to resolve at the slowest edge that still meets timing.

The upsides: a fast edge spends less time in the undefined region between logic thresholds, so it's less sensitive to noise and has less jitter, because timing error from voltage noise is noise divided by slew rate.
It gives more setup and hold margin, higher achievable data rates, and in a power switch less time with voltage and current overlapping, so lower switching loss.
The downsides all trace back to the extra high-frequency content. EMI goes up, because radiation is strong at the high harmonics.
Crosstalk goes up, since it scales with dV/dt and dI/dt. Ground bounce and supply droop get worse, since L di/dt scales with edge rate.
Trace stubs and mismatches become visible as reflections and ringing, because the edge is shorter than the trace, so you suddenly need controlled impedance and termination.
You also need more measurement bandwidth, and more careful layout. So I match the edge to the job.
If a 100 megahertz bus works with 1 nanoseconds edges I won't use 100 picoseconds.
I'd use slew-rate control or a series resistor to slow it down, and only go faster where the timing budget demands it."
